summary:
The legislative branch of the Associated Students was the Student Congress, called Congress in the document that created it. The constitution students ratified in April 1966 vested the legislative authority of the Associated Students in Congress and enumerated twenty-five seats, each attached to a constituency. Each of the four class councils sent its president, its vice president and one representative at large, twelve seats in all. Professional and honor groups, departmental clubs and general clubs sent one representative each. The Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, the men's residence halls and the women's residence halls sent two apiece. Two representatives were elected at large. The four officers of the Associated Students served as officers of Congress: the vice president, secretary and treasurer sat as voting members, and the president presided and voted only to break a tie. Officers and members took office in the second week of May and served one calendar year. Two-thirds of the total membership had to be present before Congress could consider business.

Congress gave final approval to the budget the Finance Committee prepared, approved constitutional appointments, and ruled on petitions from student organizations seeking University recognition, Greek-letter social fraternities excepted. It could delegate executive power to the Executive Council for fixed periods by a three-fourths vote, remove a member by a three-fourths vote on secret ballot, set its bylaws by two-thirds, and amend the constitution by two-thirds of its full membership followed by a majority of students voting in a regular election. Every change was subject to University approval. Three constitutional committees stood under it: Rules and Elections, Finance, and Student Activities, five members each.

The first Congress was elected in May 1966. The roster kept by the President's Office lists twenty-five people, including two Interfraternity and two Panhellenic representatives, two men's residence hall representatives and one woman's; no freshman seats appear, those being filled in the fall.

The apportionment was attacked early. The Herald reported on 20 February 1969 that Congress had voted 18 to 1 the previous week for Kent Gildersleeve's resolution to form a revision committee. Gildersleeve said clubs and professional and service fraternities with memberships as large as Greek organizations had no direct representative while the two Greek councils had two each. President Bill Straeffer said one representative stood for about forty clubs. Sophomore class president Steve Stephens cast the only vote against, calling the question hurried. The committee, capped at ten members, was to report on 8 May 1969. A proposed new constitution went back for study in November 1969 and work on it halted in January 1970. On 24 April 1970 Congress read and approved four amendments instead, one of them adding two members from each college and two more representatives at large, and put them to students on the cheerleader election ballot.

structure.fact: The constitution made the legislative branch the Student Congress, referred to throughout the text as Congress, and gave it the legislative authority of the Associated Students (Article III, Sections 1 and 3).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, printed in the College Heights Herald, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III)

structure.fact: Article III, Section 4 enumerated twenty-five Congress seats: Senior, Junior, Sophomore and Freshman Councils, three each (president, vice president, one representative at large); Professional and Honor groups one; Departmental Clubs one; General Clubs one; Interfraternity Council two; Panhellenic Council two; residence halls (men) two; residence halls (women) two; at-large representatives two.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 4)

structure.fact: Article III, Section 2 provided that the officers of the Associated Students served as the officers of Congress. The president, vice president, secretary and treasurer were elected by the student body in campus-wide elections (Article II, Section 1).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Articles II and III)

structure.fact: The vice president, the secretary and the treasurer were each made voting members of Congress. The president was a non-voting member except to resolve a tie, presided over all meetings of Congress and the Executive Council, and had to submit an agenda to the secretary at least ten days before a meeting of Congress.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article II, Sections 2-5)

structure.fact: Quorum: Congress had to have present two-thirds of its total membership for consideration of business (Article III, Section 7c).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 7)

structure.fact: Term of office: the president, vice president, secretary and treasurer and all members of Congress assumed the duties of office during the second week of May and served for one calendar year (Article IX).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article IX)

structure.fact: Qualifications for a Congress representative: enrolled full-time undergraduate; in good standing with the University; 2.0 academic standing or higher; and, except freshman class representatives, in attendance one semester immediately preceding candidacy. Upper-class representatives needed minimum semester hours including current load: sophomore 25, junior 55, senior 85 (Article III, Section 5).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 5)

structure.fact: Vacancies in Congress were filled by the electoral unit whose congressional seat was vacant, in a manner acceptable to the Rules and Elections Committee (Article III, Section 6). All other vacancies were filled by presidential appointment subject to approval of Congress (Article X).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 6; Article X)

structure.fact: Powers of Congress under Article III, Section 7b: hear and give final approval of the budget; approve constitutional appointments; extend the jurisdiction and activities of the constitutional committees when necessary; and function as a judicial body in impeachment proceedings.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 7)

structure.fact: Congress ruled on petitions from student organizations seeking University recognition, except Greek-letter social fraternities, which were subject to the governing powers granted to the Interfraternity and Panhellenic Councils by the University. A two-thirds affirmative vote recommended the petitioning group for recognition (Article III, Section 7e).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 7e)

structure.fact: Congress could delegate executive power to the Executive Council for fixed periods of time and within prescribed areas of authority by a three-fourths vote (Article III, Section 7d).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article III, Section 7d)

structure.fact: Impeachment and recall (Article XI): a member of Congress could be removed for just cause by a three-fourths vote of Congress acting as a judicial body, voting by secret ballot. Proceedings required the endorsement of at least five members of Congress, and a final vote could not be called until at least ten days after proceedings were instituted. An expelled representative could be re-admitted on petition and a three-fourths vote.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article XI)

structure.fact: Three constitutional committees were created: Rules and Elections, Finance and Student Activities. Each carried five members, at least two of them seniors during their term, with the same qualifications as members of Congress; each chairman called and presided over committee meetings and reported to Congress (Article V).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article V)

structure.fact: The Executive Council consisted of the president, vice president, secretary and treasurer plus three representatives elected by and from Congress. It carried out policies established by Congress, gave preliminary approval to the budget subject to action of Congress, and processed applications for recognition from student organizations (Article II, Section 6).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article II, Section 6)

structure.fact: Congress established its bylaws by a two-thirds vote, and amendments reported out of the Rules and Elections Committee also required two-thirds. All election laws and regulations had to be in the bylaws (Article XII).
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article XII)

structure.fact: Amendment procedure (Article XIII): a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress followed by ratification in a regular election by a majority of the student body voting. All changes in the constitution were subject to approval by the University. Article XIV made the constitution effective when approved by the University and ratified by a majority of the student body voting.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Articles XIII and XIV)

structure.fact: A Student Affairs Board sat outside the three branches: the Dean of Students as chairman, the Assistant Dean of Students, the Dean of Women, two faculty appointed by the President of the University, the president and vice president of Associated Students, the chairman of the Judicial Council, and one member appointed by and from the Executive Council. It ruled on directives or legislation issued by the branches or committees when these entered areas not specified in the constitution.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, 7 Apr 1966 (Article VI)

Fox vice president, Carmen Ann Willoughby secretary, Larry S. structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Congress of Associated Students, 1966

structure.fact: Three of the twenty-five named people on the first roster are marked as members of the Executive Council: David Arvin, Forrest (Bucky) Lanning and Marshall Peace, matching the constitution's three representatives elected by and from Congress.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Congress of Associated Students, 1966

structure.fact: Each class elected a president, vice-president, secretary, treasurer and a congressman. The 2 May 1968 results list all five posts for the senior, junior and sophomore classes; the congressman elected was the class representative at large who sat in Congress.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

structure.fact: The spring 1968 ballot carried a constitutional amendment to revise the qualifications for treasurer, alongside cheerleader and student fee questions.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Student Election Ballot, Apr 1968

structure.fact: Acting on Kent Gildersleeve's resolution, Congress elected Mike Durham (junior class representative), Doug Alexander (sophomore class vice-president) and Gildersleeve to the constitution revision committee. Two further members, one from the Judicial Council and one from the Executive Council, were to be appointed by president Bill Straeffer, and the chairman of Congress could make further appointments subject to approval of Congress on condition the committee not exceed ten members. The committee was to submit its final revision to Congress on 8 May 1969.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 48:18, 20 Feb 1969

structure.fact: The four constitutional changes read and approved by Congress on 24 April 1970 were: a change in membership and voting rights covering the right of graduate students to hold elected office, approved in a form requiring anyone running for office to be an undergraduate and to remain so throughout the tenure of office; the addition of two members from each of the colleges together with two more representatives at large; the establishment of inferior judicial councils; and impeachment of members of Congress. All four were to go on the campus cheerleader election ticket the following month.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 49:43, 24 Apr 1970

structure.fact: The seat system then in force was described in the Herald's report as a guaranteed seat system. Steve Todd, a member of the constitutional revision committee, urged Congress to consider an at-large system of representation instead; parliamentarian Phil Meyers concurred.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 49:43, 24 Apr 1970

structure.fact: Associated Student Congress Bill No. 3 established an Environmental Commission. Vice president David Porter circulated it to WKU faculty with a memo dated 15 May 1970, the bill attached. It is the earliest numbered piece of Congress legislation the archive holds for this era; data/legislation.json indexes nothing earlier than 1991-92.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Environmental Commission, David Porter, 15 May 1970

The archive has the notice that voting ran until 4 p.m. on 1 May 1970 and nothing after it; the TopSCHOLAR SGA Amendments series holds nothing between 1966 and 1976, so no adopted text survives there. (2) Whether the April 1968 amendment revising the treasurer's qualifications passed. The 3 May 1968 results memo reports offices only. (3) The size of Congress in any year after 1966-67. Only the 1966 roster of twenty-five names was found; no membership list for 1967-68, 1968-69 or 1969-70 was located, so the effect of the guaranteed-seat system on actual attendance is unknown, and the archive cannot say how many seats sat empty. (4) Attendance rules and meeting frequency. The 1966 constitution set a quorum of two-thirds and required the president's agenda ten days before a meeting, but fixed no meeting schedule and no attendance penalty; those would have sat in the bylaws Congress adopted under Article XII, and no bylaws from these years were found. The only quorum failure the Herald index shows, on 4 September 1970, falls outside this block. (5) Standing committees of Congress beyond the three constitutional ones. The Herald of 20 February 1970 reports the government enlarging its committees but the index gives no list; the item headed that Associated Students committees were listed runs on 11 September 1970, after this block. (6) The numbering of the Congresses. The archival description of the 1966 roster calls it the first Congress; no source found numbers any later one. (7) No minutes of the Congress for 1966-70 were located, in data/documents or on TopSCHOLAR. (8) Two identified sources were not read: the Western Alumnus article "Evolution of Student Government at Western" (1968, dlsc_ua_records/8543) and the Associated Student Government organization chart dated 1969 (dlsc_ua_records/510). Both would bear directly on how the branch was structured and are the first things a later pass should open. (9) The 1966 roster lists William (Winky) Menser as senior class president in the first Congress, a year before he led the Associated Students. The archive should verify his classification before drawing any conclusion from it. (10) The wider power the Herald says had recently been given to the Judicial Council by February 1969 is not described in any source found here.

summary:
The legislative body of the Associated Students was its Congress. It met weekly on Tuesday evenings: 133 sets of minutes and agendas survive for 1986-87 through spring 1992 in the SGA's own records, and of the 124 that are neither Glasgow-campus nor executive-council records, 122 are dated on a Tuesday. Two 1987-88 sets record a 5 p.m. start. The surviving minutes are uneven by session: 25 for 1986-87, 6 for 1987-88, 24 for 1988-89, 36 for 1989-90, 25 for 1990-91 and 15 for 1991-92.

Congress worked through bills and resolutions, numbered in separate series that restarted each semester with an F or S suffix. Each measure was printed on ASG letterhead with a status block for first reading, second reading, pass, fail and other, and closed with author and sponsor lines; the sponsor was usually a standing committee. Committees named in the surviving record include Student Affairs, Public Relations, Legislative Research, Academic Affairs and Campus Improvements. The president could veto; Congress could override, and rewrote the override procedure in Bill 91-6-S in spring 1991. The override was used on 14 March 1991, when the emergency-kit resolution survived a veto. Most output was a request to a named administrator, sent out as correspondence over the president's signature.

Members were elected with the executive each April, with further congress and freshman seats filled in October. Seats were also filled by filing and by vote of Congress at a meeting, and could be lost for absenteeism. In March 1988 the Herald reported that 2 of 32 congress positions were contested.

Vacancies ran through the whole period. A member lost his seat in October 1987 and Congress moved to get tough on absenteeism; a class president quit in January 1988; four positions were filled at one meeting in February 1988; ASG publicly gave its reasons for its vacancies on 23 February 1988; it filled half its open slots in November 1988; and vacancies were still on the agenda in March 1992. Congress voted to expand itself on 29 March 1990, and a February 1992 bill would have added three non-traditional seats.

Twenty years of amendments were consolidated into one document dated 4 August 1986. Amendments went to the students: 81 voted to approve a set on 12 November 1987, and one amendment failed in April 1987 for want of members present. On 19 November 1987 Congress began an impeachment process against a member; it dropped the request on 3 December and put him under a watchdog committee instead. Bill 92-10-S, introduced 1 April 1992, proposed the constitutional amendment renaming the body. Congress voted on 7 April 1992, students ratified on 14 April with about 1,200 voting, and the Student Government Association name took effect that autumn.

structure.fact: The legislative body was called Congress. Herald headlines of the period name it directly: bills passed "Congress," one member wrote most of "Congress bills," congress positions were filled at meetings, and the body voted to expand "Congress."
structure.src_label: Herald 62:46, 19 Mar 1987, "Martin Luther King Bill Passes Congress Members Split by Argument"

structure.fact: Amendments to motions had to be submitted in writing rather than raised orally, under Bill 86-2-S, introduced 28 January 1986.

structure.fact: Bill #89-01-F, introduced 5 September 1989, amended the by-laws concerning the President's Board and dealt with committee assignments.

structure.fact: Holding a paid university staff post made an officer ineligible under the ASG constitution: Amos Gott resigned as Judicial Council chairman in January 1991 after taking a part-time university job.

structure.fact: Constitutional amendments were put to the student body for ratification. On 12 November 1987, 81 students voted to approve a set of amendments.

structure.fact: Amendments also required a threshold of members present inside Congress: an amendment was defeated on 9 April 1987 because too few members turned up to vote on it.

structure.fact: Congress voted to expand itself on 29 March 1990, a week after reporting it might add representatives, so that classes and student groups would have more voice.

structure.fact: The renaming was carried out as a constitutional amendment: Bill #92-10-S, introduced 1 April 1992, was a bill to change Associated Student Government to Student Government Association.

structure.fact: Congress gave awards to its own members at a yearly banquet. The minutes of 15 March 1988 carry a description of awards listing the Dero Downing Award, Outstanding Congress Member, Outstanding Committee Member, the Dean Charles A. Landing pages and listings returned 200, but every request to cgi/viewcontent.cgi and to the /context/sga/article/.../viewcontent/ path returned an AWS WAF JavaScript challenge (HTTP 202, empty body) and then 403, including after the prescribed 90-second backoff and repeated later attempts. Two other workflows were crawling the same host. Not established: the composition of Congress as the 1986 constitution defined it, that is, how seats were apportioned between colleges, classes, residence halls and at-large constituencies. The only hard seat number found for the whole block is 32 positions in spring 1988, from a Herald headline. The seat count that resulted from the 29 March 1990 expansion is not recorded in any source found.

Not established: quorum. The April 1987 amendment failed because too few members were present, but no source found states the threshold. Term lengths for congress members are not stated in any source found, only that most seats were elected in April and some in October.

Not established: who presided over Congress in these years. No source found names a Speaker or other presiding officer for 1986-92. The 1993 bill amending the constitution gives that duty to the Vice President, but that is the September 1993 document and I have not assumed it applied earlier.

Not established: the impeachment. The Herald index preserves the headlines for 19 November 1987 (process begun), 3 December 1987 (request dropped) and 10 December 1987 (watchdog committee) but not the article text. The grounds, the constitutional provision invoked, the vote counts, and who brought the complaint are all unknown. The minutes for those weeks do not survive: the collection jumps from 17 November 1987 to 1 March 1988, and 1987-88 has only 6 surviving sets against 25 for the year before.

Not established: the outcome of the arrest reported on 17 March 1988. No charge is named in the index and no source found reports any resolution. The surname is printed as Schilling in 1986 and 1987 items and as William Byron Shilling in the arrest headline; the archive's convention is to flag this rather than pick one.

Not established: what the amendments ratified on 12 November 1987 changed, and what the amendments on the 14 April 1992 ballot changed apart from the name. The Herald indexes both as "amendments" in the plural without listing them.

Not established: any Judicial Council ruling of this period. A 1986-87 roster survives as a record but its contents were not readable, and no judicial decision, election appeal ruling or constitutional interpretation from 1986-92 was found in any source.

Not established: whether the February 1992 bill adding three non-traditional seats passed, and whether the 1990 expansion was ever implemented.

One caution for whoever edits this: the WKU Archives index labels several 1987-88 and 1988-89 items "Student Government Association" even though the body did not carry that name until fall 1992. That is the indexer's later usage, not evidence of an earlier rename.

summary:
The legislative branch was the Student Senate. It met at 5 p.m. every Tuesday, in Downing University Center 305 as of May 2010, Cravens Library 111 by 2012 while Downing was rebuilt, and the Senate Chamber on the second floor of the Downing Student Union from 2014. Quorum was a simple majority of members. Legislation took two readings, with the Legislative Research Committee reviewing every item in between and determining its constitutionality. A bill acted within the Senate's own jurisdiction; a resolution recommended university policy or stated the Senate's opinion.

The Senate held thirty-six seats across the period, redrawn twice. Until 2013 they were four senators from each of the four classes, two graduate senators, one Gatton Academy senator and seventeen at-large. Resolution 5-13-S, given its second reading on 26 February 2013 and referred to the spring ballot, cut the class seats to three each, created one senator for each of the six academic colleges, cut at-large seats to fifteen, added a seat for the president or delegated representative of each chartered regional affiliate, and wrote a Regional Affiliates article into the constitution. Resolution 1-13-F, passed 10 September 2013 and ratified in the fall election with 310 yes votes of 426 cast, created one Navitas or English as a Second Language international student senator and cut at-large seats to fourteen. Bill 1-17-S, passed 30-0 on 14 February 2017, replaced the affiliates with Regional Ambassadors nominated by each regional chancellor and confirmed by two thirds of the Senate and four of the seven executive officers, and added a South Campus liaison chosen by the president.

Attendance ran through the Judicial Council. The bylaws allowed a senator no more than three absences a semester unless the Council excused them; the Secretary of the Senate reported excessive absences to the Council and the Speaker, the member appeared to explain, and the Council decided within seven days. In November 2011 ten of thirty-six senators were called to review and two were dismissed after missing their hearings. From 17 March 2015 the bylaws required every vote to be by roll call or electronic ballot and the minutes posted within a week. Bill 4-17-S required each senator to keep one office hour a week for the rest of spring 2017.

SGA's posted legislation archive begins in fall 2011. It records 53 numbered items for 2011-12, 52 for 2012-13, 26 for 2013-14, 49 for 2014-15, 38 for 2015-16 and 63 for 2016-17. The 2013-14 figure is short: the posted spring 2014 list stops at Bill 7, while the Herald reported Bill 17-14-S passing on 1 May 2014. Spring 2017 alone reached Bill 29 and Resolution 10.

The Executive Cabinet could veto by majority vote and the Senate could override with two thirds. The posted archive records three vetoes in these years: a 2011 dance marathon bill, the 2014 smoke-free campus resolution and a 2017 resolution on the awards banquet. None was overridden, and the record shows an override vote only in the 2014 case.

structure.fact: Before the 2013 amendments the Senate was composed of four senior, four junior, four sophomore and four freshman class senators, two graduate senators, one Gatton Academy senator and seventeen at-large senators, thirty-six seats in all (Constitution 3.6).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 3.6

structure.fact: All but the four freshman senators and three at-large positions were elected in the spring; the four freshman senators, three at-large positions and the Gatton Academy senator were elected in the fall (Constitution 3.7). Vacancies after the fall elections were filled by presidential appointment with the approval of a majority of the Senate (3.8.1).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, sections 3.7-3.8

structure.fact: Senate members served one academic year. Those elected in the spring took office no later than two weeks after the fall term began; those elected in the fall took office no later than two weeks after the fall elections (Constitution 9.2, 9.3).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 9

structure.fact: The Speaker of the Senate was elected by the Senate serving in the spring semester for the next academic year, had to be at least a sophomore who had served one academic year as a senator, and had to post six office hours a week. The Secretary of the Senate was appointed by the Speaker and approved by the Senate (Constitution 3.2.4, 3.3.6, 3.3.8, 3.4.1).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, sections 3.2-3.4

structure.fact: Five standing committees existed under the constitution before 2016: Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements. Committee heads were appointed by the President and approved by a majority of the Senate (Constitution 5.1.2-5.6).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 5

structure.fact: A senator could be removed by impeachment: written endorsement of at least twenty percent of the Senate's membership to initiate, proceedings in special session presided over by the Chief Justice, no final vote sooner than fourteen days, and a two-thirds vote of the full membership of the Senate sitting as a judicial body (Constitution 3.10).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 3.10

summary:
The Associated Students kept a judicial body through the whole decade, under two names and at least four sizes. The 1971 Talisman described a seven-member Judicial Committee for 1970-71 that interpreted the constitution, heard appeals of all election disputes, ruled on student traffic violations and considered conduct questions referred by the Dean of Student Affairs. Its photograph caption named eight people and gave David Eyler as chairman. Senior listings in the same volume, and President John Lyne's own essay, called the body the Judicial Council.

Students approved a new Associated Students constitution on 10 December 1970 by 1,397 to 697, with 2,094 voting; the Herald listed strengthening the judicial system among its key issues, and the document went on to the administration and the Board of Regents. Congress passed a further revision 23 to 0 on 2 March 1972, twenty-two votes being needed to pass it, and students ratified it 157 to 16 across 29 and 30 March 1972. The Herald reported that the judicial branch had been revised to clarify judicial processes on campus and that the constitution took effect when officers were installed on 27 April 1972.

Members were appointed, not elected. In April 1972 the Herald described a five-member council made up of people appointed by president Linda Jones or former president John Lyne, chaired by John Knight. That council ruled Kim Weaver ineligible to run for president at 7 p.m. on 5 April 1972; the nine-member Student Affairs Board overruled it the next day, holding Weaver had not had a fair hearing. On 13 April five of the council's eight members disqualified themselves and it declined to hear Bob Hatfield's election appeal. The 1973 Talisman put the council at ten under Don Carter, hearing appeals on parking tickets, dorm campusing and election violations; residence-hall boards sent it about 100 conduct cases in 1971-72.

Marc Levy's charge that treasurer David Payne had spent before the budget was approved was heard on 23 October 1975 and decided for Payne. Congress opened impeachment proceedings against the council's own chairman, Gerard Faulk, on 16 March 1976, six members moving where the constitution required five. Hearings ran three weeks. On 6 April 1976 the roll call was none for removal, 12 against and 16 abstaining, with 28 members present, short of the three-fourths of full membership removal required. Faulk chaired the seven-member judicial branch listed for 1976-77. The council voted 6 to 1 on 5 October 1976 to drop the Maranatha payment case, and in April 1978 it denied Ed Johnson's appeal against Steve Thornton's election. In September 1978 Bob Moore's appointment as chairman lapsed because the constitution barred staff from the council.

summary:
The Associated Student Government's third branch in these years was the Judicial Council. The constitution divided ASG into an executive branch, a legislative branch, a judicial branch and committees, and vested the judicial authority in the council.

The council had seven regular members and three alternates. The ASG president appointed them all, subject to a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress, and named the chairman from among the seven. Appointments were due no later than two weeks after the fall term began. Members had to have been enrolled the preceding semester, hold a 2.25 academic standing, stay off disciplinary probation, remain students and not faculty or staff, sit outside Congress, and not have been a candidate for an ASG executive office in the year they were appointed. The chairman set the meetings and administered the oath of office to ASG's officers and to Congress. The council elected one alternate as clerk and kept its records in the ASG office.

The constitution listed five duties: to interpret the constitution and by-laws when the president, the Executive Council or Congress asked; to hear appeals from inferior courts; to review acts of Congress at the request of a Congress member, the president, the Executive Council or any registered student; to hear every appeal from the Rules and Elections Committee over election disputes, including qualifications for candidacy; and to set its own procedural rules. Impeachment ran through Congress, which sat as a judicial body and removed officers by a two-thirds vote of its full membership, on the written endorsement of five members, with no final vote until fourteen days had passed.

The council worked in bursts. Paul Deom was appointed in autumn 1980 and wrote in February 1982 that he had been replaced mid-term. Marcel Bush made no appointments in autumn 1981, said two of the seven seats were active when she took office, and called the council virtually non-functioning. David Payne appointed a full council in January 1982, said he understood the timing went against the constitution, and had seven members sworn in on 26 January; Margaret Ragan said it would hold one scheduled meeting a year and otherwise meet only when a controversy arose. A week later the Herald reported a conflict-of-interest row over Payne appointing his roommate to it.

Election disputes reached the council on appeal from the Rules and Elections Committee. That committee refused to certify the April 1982 general election after 989 votes were recorded against 937 signatures, and it rejected a bid to disqualify Ragan over late spending forms. Ed Kenney appealed his 1987 disqualification to the council. Bruce Cambron appealed to it in April 1988 after 380 write-in ballots were ruled invalid. A roster survives for 1986-87: seven members and three alternates, chaired by Dan Woolen. Amos Gott chaired the council in 1990-91 and left it in January 1991, ineligible after taking a part-time university job.

summary:
SGA's judicial branch in these years was the Judicial Council. The constitution vested the association's judicial authority in it. The council had five justices. The president appointed them and the senate confirmed each by a two-thirds vote; the president also named the chief justice from among the five, subject to a majority senate vote. Justices took office no later than two weeks after the fall term began and served one academic year. Vacancies were to be filled within two weeks of a resignation. A justice needed a 2.5 cumulative grade point average and could not sit in another branch of SGA. The council picked one justice as clerk, designated a justice to report to the senate twice a month, and met at least twice a month.

Its powers were written down. It interpreted the constitution and bylaws on request. It held judicial review over acts of the Executive Cabinet and the Senate at the request of any registered student not on the council. It heard election appeals and questions of candidacy. It enacted and reviewed the election codes, subject to a majority senate vote. It reviewed every constitutional amendment before the senate voted on it. It acted under the attendance policy against members brought up for review; senators were allowed no more than three absences a semester unless the council excused them. A request signed by ten students obliged the council to investigate an executive or legislative officer for censure. The chief justice presided over impeachments of executive and legislative officers, and administered the oath of office.

Most of its recorded work was elections and attendance. It supervised the annual elections under codes it wrote, ran candidate orientation, took itemised expenditure reports, and could disqualify a candidate or order a new election. In November 2009 it removed a senator for unexcused absences. In November 2011 ten of the senate's 36 members were called before it and two were dismissed. In April 2013 it disqualified the president-elect 3-2 over an election-code violation, then declined to contest a dean's memorandum reinstating her. It struck down a senate amendment in September 2013 and voided a senate motion on Talisman funding in December 2013.

Its largest single act was in February 2009. The constitution gave the executive vice president the presidency but not the Board of Regents seat, and required a special election for the seat under KRS 164.321, with the council holding discretion over timeline, applications and campaigning. The council voted 2-1 on 10 February to hold that election. Its chief justice cast the dissent and resigned two days later.

The office changed twice. Amendments adopted 26 February 2013 made a justice's term the length of the justice's academic career and extended the council's reach to regional affiliates. An amendment to raise the council to seven justices was voided in February 2014.

summary:
The judicial branch of the Student Government Association was the Judicial Council. The constitution vested SGA's judicial authority in it, set it at seven justices, and made them presidential appointees confirmed by a two-thirds vote of the Senate. A justice had to be a student in good standing, could not sit in another branch, and held the seat for the rest of an academic career while meeting the requirements. The council elected its own chief justice by majority vote, subject to a majority of the Senate; the chief justice named an associate chief justice, also confirmed by the Senate. A chief justice had to have completed a year as an associate justice, or be granted an exemption by the Senate. That was still the method in 2026.

The council did four things. It interpreted the constitution and bylaws when any registered student not on the council asked. It ruled on the absences and office hours of senators and officers. It wrote the election codes, subject to a Senate vote, ran the code meetings candidates had to attend, and heard election complaints. It held censure hearings. Quorum was five minus vacancies under the General Procedural Rules the Senate adopted in spring 2022; the bill adopting them recorded that the council had previously had no formal written procedures.

It ruled against SGA itself throughout. On 21 November 2013 it held that Bill 08-05-S of 2005, the Talisman student referendum, had never been passed by any route the bylaws authorised, was unconstitutional when passed and had never been SGA's position, which also made the Senate's vote that month to rescind it null. On 3 December 2015 it voided Bills 8-15-F and 9-15-F under Bylaw 6.1, because SGA could allocate money only to students, cancelling $1,500 for the physics department and up to $759 for art. On 3 December 2021 it held that where the constitution and the bylaws conflicted over the executive veto, the constitution governed. On 12 November 2025 it heard the entire executive cabinet's censure request against Senator Jade Ismail and refused it 7-0.

Chief justices often did not finish a year. Kelsey Luttrell resigned in December 2015, saying the council had been publicly ridiculed and lacked support. Jacob McAndrews resigned in March 2019 to run for office. Erika Puhakka stepped down in March 2021 and President Garrett Edmonds left the seat for his successor. Ellen Henderson swore in her successor in November 2024 before graduating, and Blake Graham did the same in November 2025. A 2024 amendment required a chief justice to be eligible to serve a full academic year.

The council also enlarged its own duties. Amendments in 2017 gave it a constitutional amendment committee and the job of updating the constitution, and made the chief justice interim speaker of the Senate. Amendments ratified in 2024 raised its grade point floor to 2.5, made the chief justice report weekly and keep five office hours a week, and required removal of any member censured twice in one academic year, the rule used to remove three senators on 6 November 2024.

summary:
The Associated Students of Western Kentucky University began as a document. A sixteen-member organizational committee, drawn from the class presidents and from the residence halls, departmental clubs, honor and professional groups and the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, met from November 1965 on a plan written by Dean of Students Charles Keown. President Kelly Thompson approved the finished constitution on 1 April 1966. The Herald printed it in full on 7 April. Students ratified it in a four-day vote, 1,812 to 726 on 2,538 ballots counted from the dormitories and from Thursday and Friday polling.

That constitution created four campus-wide executive officers, a Student Congress of twenty-five representative seats, a Judicial Council of seven appointed members, and three constitutional committees: Rules and Elections, Finance, and Student Activities. Seats were distributed by group, three to each of the four class councils, two each to the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, the men's and women's residence halls and the campus at large, and one each to the professional and honor groups, the departmental clubs and the general clubs. Terms ran one calendar year from the second week of May. Congress had to have two-thirds of its total membership present to transact business, and could expel a member by three-fourths secret ballot ten days after five members endorsed proceedings. Amendment took two-thirds of the full Congress, then a majority of students voting at a regular election, then the University's approval. The first Congress, elected in May 1966, seated twenty-five people: four officers and twenty-one representatives, with the freshman seats empty.

Congress reopened the text almost at once and never closed it. On 13 February 1969 it voted, 18 to 1 by the Herald's count, to create a revision committee of up to ten members. Four changes went to students in voting that closed on 1 May 1970; a quorum question went on the October 1970 ballot. A wholly new constitution carried a referendum on 10 December 1970, 1,397 to 697, after the Rules and Elections Committee refused to run the vote; it went to the administration and the record says no more about it. Congress approved a further draft on 3 March 1972, and students ratified it 157 to 16 in a two-day referendum on 29 and 30 March, on a turnout below two per cent of 10,133 students. Effective at the installation of officers on 27 April 1972, it renamed the body the Associated Student Government, split the vice presidency into administrative and activities posts, replaced the club, Greek and residence-hall seats with ten representatives-at-large and two from each academic college, and rewrote the judicial article.

Revision continued. Bill 2 created a revision committee in September 1976 and Bill 11 sent its work to a student referendum in April 1977; Congress approved a revised constitution on 30 November 1978 and passed amendments in February 1979; the 1983 revisions went on the April election ballot. By 1986 the accumulated text survived as a typed constitution of five executive officers, a Congress of class officers and college, on-campus, off-campus, at-large and freshman representatives, and a Judicial Council of seven with three alternates, bound with a separate sheet of further amendments.

structure.fact: The committee that drafted the constitution had sixteen places: the four class presidents, the sophomore and freshman vice presidents, a second senior and a second junior, and one representative each from the women's and men's residence halls, departmental clubs, general college clubs, professional and honor groups, the Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, and married students (that last seat unfilled). Dean of Students Charles Keown named them to President Kelly Thompson on 13 November 1965; the group met Tuesdays from 7 to 10 p.m.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Proposed Western Student Organization, Charles Keown, 13 and 16 Nov 1965

structure.fact: Keown's own draft, sent to Thompson on 16 November 1965, proposed a different body: a Student Association with an Assembly of 33 (four officers, three at-large representatives and two from each of thirteen groups), an Executive Council of seven, and a Judicial Committee of five. The adopted 1966 constitution used a Congress of twenty-five representative seats and a Judicial Council of seven.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Proposed Western Student Organization, proposed structure, 16 Nov 1965

structure.fact: The constitution of the Associated Students was printed in full in the College Heights Herald of 7 April 1966, page 8, under fourteen articles: Name and Membership, Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Constitutional Committees, Student Affairs Board, Advisor, Budget, Term of Office, Vacancies, Impeachment and Recall, Bylaws, Amendments, Ratification.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Herald, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article I made every full-time registered undergraduate a member of the Associated Students with equal voting rights, and divided the organisation into an Executive Branch, a Legislative Branch, committees, and a Student Affairs Board.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article I, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article II created four executive officers elected campus-wide: president, vice president, secretary and treasurer. A presidential candidate needed 45 semester hours of credit at a 2.25 grade point average, good standing, and two regular semesters in attendance; secretary and treasurer candidates needed 15 hours at 2.25. The president was a non-voting member of Congress except to break a tie; the other three officers voted.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article II, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article II, Section 6 created an Executive Council of seven: the four officers plus three representatives elected by and from Congress. It carried out Congress's policies, processed applications for recognition from student organisations other than Greek social fraternities, and gave the budget preliminary approval.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article II, Section 6, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article III, Section 4 listed twenty-five representative seats in Congress: three from each of the Senior, Junior, Sophomore and Freshman councils (president, vice president and one representative at large); one each from professional and honor groups, departmental clubs and general clubs; two each from the Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, the men's residence halls, the women's residence halls, and the campus at large.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article III, Section 4, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article III, Section 7 required two-thirds of Congress's total membership to be present for the consideration of business, and let Congress delegate executive power to the Executive Council for fixed periods by a three-fourths vote. Section 5 set representative qualifications at full-time undergraduate standing, a 2.0 average, and one semester in attendance except for freshmen, with 25, 55 and 85 hours for sophomore, junior and senior class representatives.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article III, Sections 5 and 7, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article IV created a Judicial Council of seven students appointed by the Executive Council and approved by Congress. Three took two-year terms and four took one-year terms; they took office no later than the second Thursday after fall registration and elected their own chairman and vice chairman. Members had to be juniors or seniors with a 2.25 average, and could not sit in Congress or have run for executive office that year.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article IV, Sections 1-3, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: The 1966 Judicial Council's listed powers included interpreting the constitution and bylaws on request, acting as a review board for contested enactments of Congress, hearing election disputes, passing on contested candidate qualifications, hearing student traffic violation and student conduct cases referred by the Dean of Students, and disciplining student organisations by censure, probation or suspension of recognition.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article IV, Section 4, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article V created three constitutional committees, Rules and Elections, Finance and Student Activities, each of five members, at least two of them seniors. Article VI created a nine-member Student Affairs Board: the Dean of Students as chairman, the Assistant Dean of Students, the Dean of Women, two faculty members named by the University president, the president and vice president of the Associated Students, the chairman of the Judicial Council, and one member of the Executive Council.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Articles V and VI, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article IX set the term: officers and all members of Congress took up their duties in the second week of May and served one calendar year. Article X filled vacancies by presidential appointment subject to Congress's approval. Article VII made the Dean of Students the advisor.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Articles VII, IX and X, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article XI let Congress remove any of its members for just cause by a three-fourths vote taken by secret ballot, acting as a judicial body. Proceedings needed the endorsement of at least five members, and no final vote could be called until ten days after they were instituted. An expelled representative could be readmitted by petition and a three-fourths vote.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article XI, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article XII gave Congress its bylaws by a two-thirds vote and required that all election laws and regulations be in the bylaws. Article XIII allowed amendment by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress followed by ratification at a regular election by a majority of the student body voting, with all changes subject to University approval. Article XIV made the constitution effective on University approval and a majority vote of students voting.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Articles XII-XIV, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: The ratification tally sheet held by WKU Archives breaks the 1966 vote down by polling place: yes 1,369 in the dormitories, 322 Thursday and 121 Friday, total 1,812; no 411 in the dormitories, 207 Thursday and 108 Friday, total 726. The sheet boxes 2,538 as the total vote.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Associated Student Government Constitution Ratification tally, May 1966

structure.fact: The roster of the first Congress, elected in May 1966, names twenty-five people: president Jim Haynes, vice president James E. Fox, secretary Carmen Ann Willoughby, treasurer Larry S. Heishman, and twenty-one representatives. No freshman council seats are listed and only one of the two women's residence hall seats is filled. Three representatives are marked as members of the Executive Council: David Arvin, Forrest Lanning and Marshall Peace.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Congress of Associated Students roster, 1966

structure.fact: The spring 1968 ballot put a constitutional amendment to students beside the cheerleader vote and a fee referendum. It would have required a candidate for treasurer to be an accounting or business major or minor with at least six credit hours of accounting including the current semester. The same ballot asked students to approve a $1.50 per semester registration fee increase allocated to the Associated Students for entertainment.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Student Election Ballot, April 1968

structure.fact: Congress recorded absences by roll call. The minutes of 13 February 1969 open with the roll and name the two members absent.
structure.src_label: SGA Meeting Minutes, 13 Feb 1969

structure.fact: The constitution ratified on 10 December 1970 was described by the Herald as centring on a student code of rights and a strengthened judicial system, and as calling for a second vice president to handle entertainment, a restructured Congress and more financial autonomy. The document was to be sent to the University administration and then to the Board of Regents.
structure.src_label: Herald 50:27, 11 Dec 1970

structure.fact: The constitution ratified on 29 and 30 March 1972 changed the organisation's name from Associated Students to Associated Student Government. Years 1972-73 onward in data/years.json still carry the org label "Associated Students".
structure.src_label: Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The 1972 constitution created two vice presidencies where one had existed. The administrative vice president deputised for the president, coordinated all committees and assisted the president; the activities and programs vice president handled publicity and coordinated social and cultural activities.
structure.src_label: Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The 1972 constitution rebuilt Congress on ten representatives-at-large plus two representatives-at-large from each academic college, and removed the seats held by the Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, the residence halls, the general clubs and the professional and honor groups. It took effect immediately after the installation of the new officers, set for 27 April 1972, and the Herald called it the culmination of eighteen months of deliberation by two bodies of Congress.
structure.src_label: Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The organisation chart for 1976-77 shows the three branches as the 1972 constitution left them: an executive of president, administrative vice president, activities vice president, treasurer and secretary; a Judicial Branch of seven members and three alternates under chairman Gerard Faulk; and a legislative branch of eight class officers, college representatives, ten representatives-at-large and twelve Academic Council representatives. The same chart lists eight dismissals, three resignations and six appointments during the year.
structure.src_label: SGA Organization Chart, 1976-77

structure.fact: Two resolutions sought a new executive office after the Board of Regents transferred concerts and lectures to the University Center Board in March 1979. Resolution 79-18, dated 26 February 1980, supported amending the constitution to include a Vice President of Public Affairs; Resolution 80-14, dated 21 October 1980, again proposed creating the post.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolutions 79-18 and 80-14

structure.fact: Congress abolished its own Finance Committee by Bill 85-1-F on 17 September 1985, created a Financial Advisory Council by Bill 85-2-F on 1 October 1985, and wrote the council into the bylaws by Bill 86-3-S on 28 January 1986. The dates in data/years.json for the first and third of these (24 September 1985 and 2 April 1986) do not match the dates TopSCHOLAR gives.
structure.src_label: SGA Bills 85-1-F, 85-2-F and 86-3-S

structure.fact: The typed constitution TopSCHOLAR holds as the 1986 consolidation lists five executive officers elected campus-wide: President, Administrative Vice-President, Public Relations Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer. Candidates needed a 2.35 average, two full semesters at Western and 30 hours in the preceding semester; the President and Administrative Vice-President had to be full-time students, and the Treasurer had to have completed three hours of accounting.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article II

structure.fact: Under the consolidated text, Congress was composed of the president and vice president of each of the four classes, one Academic Council representative and one alternate from each academic college (Potter, Ogden, Business, Graduate and Education), five on-campus representatives, five off-campus representatives, five representatives-at-large, two freshman representatives elected each fall, and the five executive officers. All but the freshman seats were elected campus-wide in the spring.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article III, Sections 4-6

structure.fact: The consolidated text lowered the removal threshold. Executive officers and members of Congress could be removed for just cause by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress on the written endorsement of five members, with no final vote for fourteen days. Judicial Council members required a three-fourths vote, on the endorsement of five members of Congress or five of the Judicial Council. The 1966 requirement that two-thirds of Congress be present for business does not appear in the text.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Articles II, III and IV

structure.fact: Under the consolidated text the Judicial Council had seven regular members and three alternates appointed by the President with a two-thirds vote of Congress, took office within two weeks of the start of the fall term, and had a chairman appointed by the President from the seven rather than elected by the Council. Its powers included judicial review of acts of Congress on the request of a member, the President, the Executive Council or any registered student. The 1986-87 roster names seven members and three alternates, with Dan Woolen as chair.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article IV; Judicial Council Roster 1986-87

structure.fact: The consolidated text named three constitutional committees: Legislative Research, Rules and Elections, and Student Affairs. The Legislative Research Committee collected and reviewed all proposed legislation after its first reading, determined the constitutionality of legislation and checked it against previous legislation. The amendment sheet bound with the document adds five more standing committees: Delegate, Student Services, Student Rights, Academic Affairs and Public Relations.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article V and amendment sheet

structure.fact: The consolidated text kept the 1966 amendment rule almost word for word: a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress, then ratification in a referendum by a majority of the student body voting, with all changes subject to University approval. Its ratification article added a third condition, that the constitution took effect at the installation of the officers elected at the next regular election.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Articles IX and X

structure.fact: The amendment sheet bound with the consolidated constitution is signed by five authors, Lynn Groemling, Daniel Duffy, Kevin Hargrave, Van C. Hodge and Robin Kinman, and sponsored by the Legislative Research, Student Affairs and Student Rights committees. It would have raised the freshman representatives from two to four, added one delegate from every university-recognised organisation, and tied quorum to the number of organisations sending a delegate.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, amendment sheet

structure.fact: The by-laws were rewritten in a run of bills across the period: 89-01-F, 89-02-F and 89-03-F on 5 September 1989 on the President's Board, on legislation and on the order of business; 90-1-F on sponsorship of bills and resolutions; 91-4-S suspending the by-laws, 91-5-S amending how resolutions were submitted, 91-6-S on overriding a presidential veto, and 91-07-F on mandatory legislation.

unanswered:
What became of the constitution students ratified on 10 December 1970. The Herald says it was going to the administration and then the Board of Regents; nothing in the archive records either acting on it. Revision work resumed in January and February 1971 and produced a different document sixteen months later, and the Herald of 31 March 1972 calls that one the work of two bodies of Congress. Whether the 1970 text was rejected, withdrawn or simply absorbed is not established.

How the April 1968 treasurer amendment was decided. The ballot survives with its text; Ron Beck's results memo of 3 May 1968 reports every officer race and the 2,894 turnout but is silent on both the amendment and the $1.50 fee question on the same ballot.

The substance of most amendments. The archive holds headlines and not texts for the four changes voted on 1 May 1970, the October 1970 quorum question, the amendment that passed at the fall 1971 freshman election, the amendments on the November 1973 ballot, the constitution amendments passed on 8 February 1979, the revised constitution approved on 30 November 1978, and the 1983 revisions. No copy of any of them was found.

The date the typed 1986 constitution actually reflects. TopSCHOLAR dates the item 4 August 1986, but its Article II, Section 3 makes the ASG President the student member of the Board of Regents, with a special election only if the President is not a Kentucky resident, while the Herald of 3 February 1983 carried President Margaret Ragan explaining that the presidency and the regent seat were then separate. Either the typed base text predates 1983 or the archive's account of the split needs revisiting. The amendment sheet bound with it carries no date at all, and three of its five authors are people the record places in 1988 to 1991.

Whether the 1986 consolidation was ever ratified. Its own Article X required University approval, a majority of students voting, and installation of the next officers. No referendum on it appears in the Herald index.

No by-laws survive for this period. The earliest by-laws in the TopSCHOLAR SGA collection are dated 1994, although the 1966 constitution required that all election laws and regulations live in the by-laws and bills amended them repeatedly from 1986 onward.

Judicial Council membership is documented for two years only, 1976-77 and 1986-87. Nothing in the archive shows when the Council changed from electing its own chairman under the 1966 text to having one appointed by the President as in the consolidated text, or when it gained three alternates; the seven-plus-three structure is already visible in 1976-77.

A large body of material was not worked in this run. TopSCHOLAR holds 843 sets of SGA minutes, of which about 240 fall between 1976 and 1992, including runs of 27 meetings in 1982 and 1983 and 34 in 1989. Those minutes would settle most of the questions above. digitalcommons.wku.edu blocks direct PDF downloads with an AWS WAF challenge; every document read here was retrieved through the Wayback Machine copy of the same file.

summary:
The Associated Students voted on 7 April 1992 to rename itself the Student Government Association. Students ratified the change in a referendum on 14 April 1992 and the name took effect that autumn. Nothing else in the governing documents changed with it.

The constitution SGA worked under for the rest of the decade was headed "As amended Spring 2001 Semester" and carried six numbered amendments after its text. Its opening clause made every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in SGA elections. It named three branches: an executive branch of five elected officers, a legislative branch called Congress, and a five-member Judicial Council appointed by the president. Congress seats were tied to constituencies, among them classes, residence halls apportioned one to four by population, academic colleges, graduate, non-traditional, off-campus and at-large members, and the committee chairs the president appointed sat in it as well. Amendments required two-thirds of Congress and a student referendum, and every change also needed the university administration's approval. The sixth amendment, a Supremacy Clause, passed at the spring 2002 general election.

In February 2003 Congress passed Bill 03-5-S, putting a $3-a-semester fee for the campus radio station on the April general election ballot. Students approved it 1,066 to 765 of 2,014 voting, and it went to the Board of Regents, which took up radio station fees at its 9 May 2003 quarterly meeting. The Herald reported it as the first student referendum in SGA's history; the archive also holds earlier constitutional referenda. The route it set, in which the body puts a fee to students and a yes vote becomes a request to the regents, was used again in March 2005 for a $9 Talisman yearbook fee, approved 1,019 to 669, and in October 2006 on the move to Division I-A football.

Robert Watkins, chair of the Legislative Research Committee, wrote a new constitution and bylaws in autumn 2003 after reviewing other universities' documents. Four attempts to pass them failed because two-thirds of Congress was not present. Congress passed them unanimously on 10 February 2004 with 25 of 29 members there, after the Judicial Council struck about 13 members from the roll for absences. In the ratifying referendum of 9 March 2004, 132 students voted, 116 for and 16 against, from an enrolment of about 18,000. The documents took effect in fall 2004. Congress became the Senate and fell from 75 seats to 35; seats vacant after the fall elections could still be filled by presidential appointment. The vice presidencies of finance and public relations were abolished, and a Chief of Staff, Speaker of the Senate, Secretary of the Senate, Director of Information Technology and Director of Academic and Student Affairs were created. Executive officers were barred from proposing legislation. Nine students stood for the 28 spring senate seats that month.

A referendum in March 2005 adopted 40 further amendments, 1,193 to 262. SGA published the resulting documents as its constitution and bylaws.

structure.fact: The governing document in force before 2004 was headed "Constitution for the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University, As amended Spring 2001 Semester," with six numbered amendments printed after the main text.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as amended Spring 2001 (Wayback capture, 5 Nov 2004)

structure.fact: Clause 1.1 of the Spring 2001 constitution already made all enrolled students members of SGA with the right to vote in all its elections. The archive elsewhere credits that provision to the 2004 constitution, following SGA's history page; the 2001 text carries it word for word.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as amended Spring 2001, clause 1.1 (Wayback capture, 5 Nov 2004)

structure.fact: Under the Spring 2001 constitution the executive branch consisted of five elected officers: President, Executive Vice President, Vice President of Finance, Vice President of Public Relations and Vice President of Administration. The Vice President of Finance had to have completed at least three hours of accounting on taking office.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as amended Spring 2001, clauses 2.1 and 2.2.6 (Wayback capture, 5 Nov 2004)

structure.fact: The Spring 2001 constitution's base text composed Congress of five non-traditional and five graduate representatives, ten from each of the four classes, residence hall representatives apportioned one to four by hall population, ten at-large members, one Academic Council representative per college appointed by the president, and the Coordinator of Committees and every standing and ad hoc committee chair, also appointed by the president.

structure.fact: Amendment 3 to the Spring 2001 constitution replaced that composition with two graduate representatives, two from each class, residence hall representatives on the same one-to-four scale, ten at-large, five off-campus, two from each academic college, and the Coordinator of Committees and committee chairs. Academic college representatives needed a 2.75 overall and a 3.0 major grade point average.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as amended Spring 2001, Amendment 3 (Wayback capture, 5 Nov 2004)

structure.fact: The Spring 2001 constitution required a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress and subsequent ratification in a referendum by a majority of students voting to amend it, and clause 9.2 made all constitutional changes subject to approval by the university administration.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as amended Spring 2001, clauses 9.1 and 9.2 (Wayback capture, 5 Nov 2004)

structure.fact: The Spring 2001 constitution named six constitutional committees: the Committee on Committees, Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as amended Spring 2001, section 5 (Wayback capture, 5 Nov 2004)

structure.fact: Amendment 6, the Supremacy Clause, made the constitution the supreme law of SGA, subordinate to the United States and Kentucky constitutions, federal, state and local law and established university policy, and made every Congress member, executive officer and justice responsible for knowing its contents. SGA's own results page recorded it as passed at the spring 2002 general election, without a vote total.

structure.fact: The 2004 constitution is headed "As Proposed Fall 2003" and names three branches: an Executive Cabinet of seven, the Student Senate, and the Judicial Council. The three elected offices were President, Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President; the Chief of Staff, Director of Public Relations, Director of Information Technology and Director of Academic and Student Affairs were appointed and all seven had a vote in the cabinet.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 1.2, 2.1 and 2.10 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The 2004 constitution set the Senate at 35 seats: four representatives from each of the senior, junior, sophomore and freshman classes, two graduate students and seventeen at-large. All but the four freshman seats and three at-large seats were elected in the spring; unfilled graduate seats converted to at-large seats at the fall elections. Vacancies after the fall elections were filled by presidential appointment with a majority of the Senate.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 3.6, 3.7 and 3.9 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: Under the 2004 constitution the Speaker of the Senate was elected from the elected Senate by the previous semester's legislative branch, served as Coordinator of Committees, and appointed the Secretary of the Senate subject to Senate approval. Committee chairs were appointed by the Speaker with a majority vote of the Senate.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 3.2.4, 3.3, 3.4 and 5.3-5.7 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The 2004 constitution named five standing committees as part of the legislative branch: Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements. It also created an Organizational-Aid Board of five members appointed by the President and approved by the Senate, a body absent from the Spring 2001 constitution.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 5 and 6 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The Executive Cabinet held a veto over all Senate legislation, carried by a majority of the cabinet, with written reasons to the sponsoring committee within forty-eight hours. The 2004 constitution set the override at three-fourths of the Senate while the 2004 bylaws set it at two-thirds of those present and voting, an inconsistency between the two documents.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 2.10.4 and 3.8.9, and bylaws as proposed Fall 2003, Article VI section 3 (Wayback captures, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: Impeachment of any executive officer, senator or justice required a written endorsement of at least twenty percent of the Senate's membership to initiate, a special session presided over by the Chief Justice (by the Speaker for justices), a final vote no sooner than fourteen days after proceedings began, and a two-thirds vote of the full Senate membership sitting as a judicial body.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 2.12, 3.10 and 4.6 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The 2004 bylaws set quorum at a simple majority of Senate members, allowed senators no more than four absences a semester unless excused by the Judicial Council, fixed Senate meetings at 5 p.m. every Tuesday, and required every senator except the Speaker and the University Senate representatives to serve on at least one committee.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA bylaws as proposed Fall 2003, Articles III, IV, V and VIII (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The 2004 constitution put a five-justice Judicial Council, appointed by the President with a two-thirds vote of the Senate, in office no later than two weeks after the start of the fall term for one academic year. The council had to meet at least twice a month, adjudicate election appeals, and review all constitutional amendments before the Senate voted on them.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 4.3 and 4.5 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: On a presidential vacancy the 2004 constitution gave the President's duties to the Executive Vice President but sent the Student Regent seat to a special election of the student body, as required by KRS 164.321, with the Judicial Council controlling the timeline, applications and campaigning. The Spring 2001 constitution had filled the whole office, regent seat included, by special election.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, sections 2.11.1-2.11.3 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The 2004 constitution kept the amendment rule at two-thirds of the full Senate membership plus a referendum of a majority of students voting, but dropped the Spring 2001 clause subjecting all constitutional changes to the approval of the university administration.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Fall 2003, section 10.1 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: The 2004 Election Codes, adopted 22 January 2004, gave the Judicial Council supervision of all elections, set filing between 1 February and 2 March, made a candidate orientation on 17 February compulsory on pain of disqualification, and capped spending at $450 for president, $400 for executive vice president, $350 for other executive offices and $50 for legislative candidates, with no single donor giving more than $100.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA, 2004 Election Codes, adopted 22 Jan 2004 (Wayback capture, 7 Sep 2004)

structure.fact: Students adopted a list of 40 amendments to the SGA constitution, compiled by the Legislative Research Committee, by 1,193 votes to 262 at the March 2005 general election. The Talisman fee question on the same ballot passed 1,019 to 669, and all 25 senate candidates were elected to 28 open seats.
structure.src_label: Herald, 17 Mar 2005, "Dawson elected SGA president" (Wayback)

structure.fact: The document SGA afterwards published as its constitution is headed "As Proposed Spring 2005." Against the 2004 text it raised the grade point average for a senate seat and for senate office from 2.0 to 2.5, lowered the veto override from three-fourths to two-thirds, moved appointment of committee chairs from the Speaker to the President, raised the Speaker's minimum office hours from five to eight a week, seated the Speaker on the Executive Cabinet as an ex-officio non-voting member, and required the Speaker to be at least a sophomore with a year's service as a senator.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Spring 2005 (Wayback capture, 11 Sep 2006)

structure.fact: The Spring 2005 constitution added two removal procedures the 2004 document lacked: removal of a committee head, with the vice-chair acting until a replacement was appointed, and a vote of no confidence in the Speaker of the Senate, with the Legislative Research Committee head serving as interim Speaker. Both used the same twenty percent endorsement, fourteen-day and two-thirds thresholds as impeachment.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA constitution as proposed Spring 2005, sections 3.11 and 3.12 (Wayback capture, 11 Sep 2006)

structure.fact: The Spring 2005 bylaws cut the permitted absences for a senator from four a semester to three, raised the number of student University Senate representatives reporting to the Senate from three to five, required authors to attend a Legislative Research Committee meeting and defend their legislation within two weeks, corrected the fiscal record-keeping reference from Bill 03-03-S to Bill 02-07-F, and set their own ratification for fall 2005.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA bylaws as proposed for Spring 2005 (Wayback capture, 11 Sep 2006)
