TopSCHOLAR's description of the 9 May 2003 quarterly minutes lists "library, facility improvement and radio station fees" among the agenda items, but the minutes PDF itself returned a bot-check (HTTP 202, then 403) on every attempt, and no Herald or Daily News report of the board's vote was found. The same is true of the $9 Talisman fee approved by students in March 2005: the archive records the request to the regents and not their answer.

2. The exact content of the 40 amendments ratified in March 2005. The Herald reports the number, the compiler (the Legislative Research Committee) and the vote. SGA's website afterwards published a constitution headed "As Proposed Spring 2005," and the differences between it and the 2004 text are set out above, but no source found states that the posted document is the 40-amendment package, and no separate list of the 40 survives in anything reachable.

3. Whether the Spring 2005 bylaws were in fact ratified. Their own Article XI says they take effect on approval by two-thirds of the legislative branch, "for the Fall 2005," and SGA's site published them, but no minutes or Herald report of the ratifying vote was found. The file also still carries the old "As Proposed Fall 2003" heading in its first line, which is a drafting leftover rather than evidence of date.

4. What the senate numbering counts. SGA's minutes call the 2006-07 body "the fifth Student Government Association." No source found says what the first was, and counting back five years from 2006-07 does not land on 2004, when the Senate was created. No numbered session is recorded in the archive before or after 2006-07.

5. When the Senate grew past 35 seats. The 2004 and Spring 2005 constitutions both fix 35. The 2006-07 minutes show a 31-seat roster, the 2009-10 minutes 32 and then 30, and by spring 2011 the Herald reports 36 open seats and 50 members. No amendment changing the seat count between 2005 and 2010 was found; the intervening documents on wku.edu/sga in the Wayback record date from 2012.

6. The record is silent on the governing documents between spring 2005 and 2010. No constitutional amendment, bylaw amendment or election-code revision from 2006 through 2010 turned up in the Herald's WordPress archive (which has a gap for the media.www years), in the Wayback captures of SGA's site, or in the legislation held locally. That is an absence of evidence, not evidence that nothing happened.

7. Detail on the 1990s amendments. The archive records constitutional amendments on the ballot in April 1996 and a Bill 93-1-F proposing amendments in September 1993, but no text of either survives in anything reachable, so what they changed is unknown. The same applies to the September 1999 bill said to have amended the constitution to include website guidelines.

8. One correction to flag for the editor. The archive's entry dated 2004-01-01 credits the 2004 constitution with making every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote, following SGA's own history page. The Spring 2001 constitution already carried that provision as clause 1.1, word for word. The 2004 document restated it; it did not introduce it.

summary:
Two documents governed the Student Government Association through these years. The constitution set the three branches, the executive offices, the Senate's seats and the removal procedures, and could be changed only by a Senate vote followed by a student referendum. The bylaws set meeting procedure, attendance and committee rules, and the Senate amended them on its own vote.

On 26 February 2013 the Senate gave Resolution 5-13-S, written by President Cory Dodds, a second reading and referred it to the spring ballot. It cut each class delegation from four senators to three, added one senator elected by each academic college, cut at-large seats from seventeen to fifteen, extended Judicial Council terms from one year to the length of a justice's academic career, and reduced the Organizational Aid Board from ten members to six. A fall 2013 referendum adding a Navitas and English as a Second Language international seat drew 426 votes, 310 of them yes.

Committees entered the constitution one at a time. Sustainability and MyCampusToo, renamed the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion, were made permanent on bills read 15 November 2016; SAVES followed on 4 April 2017. That same night the Senate voted 24-7 to cut the membership grade point average floor from 2.5 to 2.0, and on 19 April students ratified six amendments. The text reissued as amended spring 2017 carried a 36-seat Senate, eight standing committees, and a seven-justice Judicial Council appointed by the president on a two-thirds Senate vote.

Bill 8-20-S, read on 14 April 2020 with campus closed by COVID-19, set out emergency clauses: officers and senators could hold over until an election could be run, and the president could hold the student regent's seat. Those clauses became Section 11 of the constitution.

The text WKU posted for 2023-24 was a different document. It listed seven committees under new names and thirty-seven Senate seats, among them transfer, first-generation and Intercultural Student Engagement Center seats. Three measures from the Legislative Operations Committee, read that November, corrected the documents against themselves: University Senate became Faculty Senate because that body had split in two, committee names were brought into line with names the Senate had already changed, and the bylaws sections on expelling senators were struck because the constitution provided only for impeachment.

On 28 March 2024 the Senate voted a package of amendments drafted by a committee under Chief Justice Isaac King. It renamed the vice presidencies Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, struck two directorships, raised the grade point average floors to 2.5 for senators and 2.75 for the cabinet, required removal after a second censure in one academic year, moved committee-head appointments from the president to the speaker, and changed the amendment rule from two-thirds of the full Senate to two-thirds of the senators present. Students renamed the diversity committee the Action and Opportunity Committee by referendum in April 2025, 88 per cent in favour. The Senate adopted a codified rewrite of the bylaws on 24 February 2026.

structure.src_label: SGA Bill 17-22-S
